summary: Updates the cipher suites required for sending syslog messages securely over TLS and DTLS. It changes requirements set in the TLS and DTLS transport mappings for syslog, and updates the protocol recommended for secure datagram transport.

eli5.summary: Computers write diary entries called logs and send them over the network in a locked box. This swaps the old locks for newer, stronger ones.

questions: which cipher suites for syslog over tls
which cipher suite should secure syslog use
is tls 1.3 early data allowed for syslog
subtitle: Secure syslog gets a forward-secret cipher suite and drops DTLS 1.0, without cutting off older devices.

tldr.problem: The secure syslog specifications require a cipher suite without forward secrecy, and one of them requires DTLS 1.0, which has been deprecated.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9662 makes TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 a required cipher suite beside the old one, says to prefer it, requires DTLS 1.2 instead of DTLS 1.0, and forbids TLS 1.3 early data.
tldr.outcome: Old and new devices can still interoperate during a migration, while implementations are steered towards forward secrecy.

today: RFC 9662 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024. It updates RFC 5425 and RFC 6012, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Secure Syslog Needs an Update
sections.content:
RFC 5425 and RFC 6012 describe how to carry syslog messages securely over TLS and DTLS. Both require the cipher suite TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA and both rely on RSA-based certificates and on versions of TLS and DTLS that are not the most recent.

RFC 5425 requires TLS 1.2. RFC 6012 requires DTLS 1.0. This document updates both RFCs to prefer TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 over the old suite, and it also recommends a mandatory-to-implement secure datagram transport for RFC 6012.
sections.eli5: Two older rule books for sending logs safely use locks that are now considered old. This new note says to use a better lock when you can.

sections.title: The Case for Moving On
sections.content:
The RFC gives several reasons. TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA does not provide forward secrecy, a feature the text calls highly desirable for securing event messages. It may also need mitigation techniques that can be hard to implement well. TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 does provide forward secrecy.

Moving does not force operators to replace certificates. ECDHE cipher suites exist for both RSA and ECDSA certificates, so the RSA certificates already installed in devices can stay. Separately, DTLS 1.0 was deprecated by RFC 8996, so the transport that RFC 6012 made mandatory must change.

The text also notes that many syslog implementations use the suite mandated by RFC 6012, so a sudden change is not desirable. During the migration either suite may be used, but it is REQUIRED that TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 be preferred.
sections.eli5: The old lock can be picked in some tricky ways and does not protect yesterday's messages if someone steals the key later. The new lock fixes that, and your old keys still fit the door.

sections.title: New Rules for Syslog over TLS
sections.content:
For RFC 5425, the mandatory-to-implement cipher suites are now REQUIRED to be TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. Implementations SHOULD offer the ECDHE suite but MAY offer the older one.

TLS 1.2 stays the mandatory-to-implement transport protocol. Following RFC 9325, implementations SHOULD support TLS 1.3 and, if they implement it, MUST prefer to negotiate it over earlier versions.
sections.eli5: Everyone must know how to use both locks. When you can, offer the new one first, and use the newest kind of lockbox if you have it.

sections.title: New Rules for Syslog over DTLS
sections.content:
For RFC 6012, the cipher suite rules are the same as for TLS: both suites are REQUIRED to be implemented, and implementations SHOULD offer the ECDHE suite but MAY offer the older one.

The transport rule changes more. Implementations MUST NOT use DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) and MUST use DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347). DTLS 1.2 implementations SHOULD support and prefer TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. Implementations SHOULD also support DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147) and, if implemented, MUST prefer to negotiate it over earlier DTLS versions.
sections.eli5: The old version of the secure postcard service is switched off. The next version is now the one everybody must be able to use, and an even newer one is welcome.

sections.title: No Early Data
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 has a mechanism called early data (also called 0-RTT data) that lets a client send data in its first flight of messages, using a pre-shared key. The RFC points out that early data is not forward secret and has no protection against replay between connections.

Syslog does not support replay protection, and most implementations keep a long-lived connection anyway. So this document specifies that implementations MUST NOT use early data.
sections.eli5: Sending a message before the secret handshake is finished is fast but risky, because a copycat could replay it. Since log connections stay open for a long time, nothing is lost by waiting, so it is not allowed.

sections.title: Security and Migration
sections.content:
Earlier RFCs deprecated an insecure DTLS version and insecure cipher suites, but the installed base of syslog implementations cannot easily be updated at once. This document therefore lets TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA stay as a required suite while directing implementations to prefer the ECDHE suite.

If a device currently only has the old suite, an administrator should evaluate the conditions and decide whether to keep allowing it, so syslog messages keep flowing until the device is updated. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If an old device cannot use the new lock yet, a grown-up decides whether it is safe enough to keep using the old one for a while.
